records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding reported in downtown Tyler.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Heavy rains in the city of Houston produced flash flooding.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fire Department preformed over 10 different water rescues across the Houston area.||TxDOT also reported flash flooding near I-45 and I-610. Areas west of I-45 from Telephone Rd to Roe Dr were indicated as flooded. TxDOT noted that water was covering the roadway along the westbound frontage road.||A Storm chaser also shared a video on social media, showing flooding at I-45 south and Wayside Drive. Significant inundation can be seen in the video with two cars stalled.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Multiple supercell thunderstorms developed along a broad, diffuse baroclinic boundary across Northeast Texas throughout the day on June 8th. MLCAPE values were in excess of 4500 J/kg in proximity to these thunderstorms, with modest northwesterly mid-level flow contributing to 45 knots of effective bulk shear. Given the very weak convective inhibition, these thunderstorms persisted for several hours from early afternoon and throughout the evening. As a result, multiple severe reports of large hail and higher end damaging wind gusts were recorded across parts of Northeast Texas along with an isolated report of flash flooding in Mount Pleasant.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding reported in Mount Pleasant via Mping.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary boundary draped across Southeast New Mexico and West Texas became a focus for shower and thunderstorm development during the afternoon of the 29th. A few storms produced damaging wind gusts, and some urban flooding was reported in Odessa.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS employee reported a stalled vehicle in 1-2 feet of water over the road at Highway 385 (Andrews Highway) and 52nd Street in Odessa. The total time of occurrence is partially estimated by radar. The cost of damages is also estimated.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of June 6th, a discrete supercell developed in southeastern Colorado and tracked into the Oklahoma Panhandle and northeastern Texas Panhandle. This supercell produced six tornadoes, hail up to 4.5 inches in diameter, and straight-line winds. Later in the evening a couple of semi-discrete supercells moved into the Oklahoma Panhandle and eastern Panhandles, producing wind gusts up to 90 mph and hail up to the size of golf balls.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Main Avenue in Gruver was covered in water.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of June 6th, a discrete supercell developed in southeastern Colorado and tracked into the Oklahoma Panhandle and northeastern Texas Panhandle. This supercell produced six tornadoes, hail up to 4.5 inches in diameter, and straight-line winds. Later in the evening a couple of semi-discrete supercells moved into the Oklahoma Panhandle and eastern Panhandles, producing wind gusts up to 90 mph and hail up to the size of golf balls.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Both directions of I-40 at Hope Road were  closed due to water over the roadway.  Traffic was being detoured to the frontage  road.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon and evening hours of the fifth, an intense supercell thunderstorm moved over the South Plains region of West Texas, producing several tornadoes over portions of Cochran, Hockley, and Lubbock Counties. This thunderstorm also produced widespread damage from very strong straight-line winds and large hail across western and southwestern portions of the City of Lubbock (Lubbock County) before it exited into Crosby and Garza Counties and weakened late in the evening. A cold front stalled south of the South Plains early in the afternoon before returning northward as a warm front. Very humid air returned to the region as the front moved northward and contributed to extreme atmospheric instability by the afternoon. This allowed for explosive thunderstorm development from far east-central New Mexico into the South Plains. This supercell initially produced a brief tornado over far northwestern Cochran County that moved over open country and produced no known damage. Shortly thereafter, the supercell produced a strong wedge-type tornado several miles northwest of Morton (Cochran County), which destroyed multiple large wooden power poles as it tracked eastward, eventually crossing Texas State Highway 214 about four miles north of Morton before dissipating over northeastern Cochran County. The supercell then produced another strong tornado over far northwestern Hockley County, about five miles northwest of the community of Pettit (Hockley County), which was directly observed by mobile research radar. A separate and very brief cone-type tornado was then observed only two miles north of Pettit. The supercell then began to track more southeastward, with no tornadoes observed for a period of approximately 15 minutes. Just as the supercell approached US Highway 385 in north-central Hockley County, it produced another strong tornado which crossed US Highway 385 about three miles south of the community of Whitharral (Hockley County). This tornado destroyed several additional wooden power poles, rolled a semi-truck traveling on the highway, and damaged buildings and trees along its path before dissipating about seven miles east of US Highway 385. The final three tornadoes produced by this supercell were observed as the storm crossed from eastern Hockley County into western Lubbock County. The first tornado developed approximately three miles northeast of Texas State Highway 114 and the community of Smyer (Hockley County), damaging and destroying multiple manufactured homes as it moved eastward before dissipating along the Hockley/Lubbock County line. The second tornado developed very close to the termination of the previous tornado, and damaged and destroyed several homes and buildings as it tracked southeastward and dissipated only about a quarter mile north of Texas State Highway 114. The final tornado produced during this event developed and tracked over southern portions of Reese Center (Lubbock County), toppling large trees and damaging roofs before dissipating just outside the Lubbock city limits. Although the storm did not produce any additional tornadoes after this point, the supercell did continue to produce very strong straight-line winds and large hail, which resulted in widespread damage to homes and businesses across western and southwestern portions of the City of Lubbock. Many buildings within the city experienced significant damage to roofs and windows, and hail up to the size of tennis balls was observed within the city limits. The supercell continued to produce large hail and severe wind gusts as it moved over the community of Slaton in southeastern Lubbock County, with the storm finally weakening over Crosby and Garza Counties with no additional severe weather reports after it moved to the east of the Caprock Escarpment. After the initial supercell thunderstorm moved east, additional thunderstorms developed over far eastern New Mexico and the South Plains bringing more severe storms late in the evening through the early morning hours of the sixth.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: An intense and long-lived supercell thunderstorm slowly tracked to the east across portions of Hockley, Lamb, Hale, Lubbock, and Crosby Counties. In addition to producing very large hail and numerous tornadoes, it also created very heavy rainfall which led to flash flooding across a large area of the South Plains. Several reports were received from storm chasers across Hockley, Lamb, and Hale Counties of water over many roadways. Numerous reports from Lubbock County and area web cams showed water flowing over city streets as deep as three feet in some areas.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An axis of training thunderstorms containing localized 3-4 inch per hour rainfall rates occurred along a well defined cold pool across parts of Central Texas and more isolated into parts of East Texas on the morning of June 12th. These thunderstorms resulted in localized heavy rainfall amounts across parts of Cherokee County. Thunderstorm inflow was characterized by 1500-3000 J/kg of MLCAPE, minimal CIN, 2-2.25 inch precipitable water values. As a result, this environment continued to foster even more thunderstorms upwind of the primary complex, which began to train given the parallel orientation of the steering flow to the cold pool and led to an isolated flash flooding report in Cherokee County.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding reported with County Road 4211 closed due to water over the road.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the early to late evening hours on the 4th of June severe thunderstorms moved through the southwest to south central Texas Panhandle. The main supercell that moved in first from eastern New Mexico, quickly intensified in Deaf Smith County, where it briefly produced a weak tornado that overturned a couple of irrigation pivots. The storm then continued to produce ping pong ball to even an instance of baseball size hail as it moved into Randall County.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rain occurred in Palo Duro Canyon, which resulted in flash flooding. The flooding closed a portion of the main road going through the canyon.

Several reports were received from storm chasers across Hockley, Lamb, and Hale Counties of water over many roadways. Numerous reports from Lubbock County and area web cams showed water flowing over city streets as deep as three feet in some areas.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Isolated to widely scattered thunderstorms developed on the afternoon of the 17th with convective temperatures breached by mid-afternoon. Although the environment was not favorable for severe storms with warm mid-level temperatures, a relatively dry sub-cloud layer allowed a few of these storms to produce severe wind gusts. The most notable storm occurred over the city of Lubbock where a peak wind gust of 77 mph was recorded. This storm also damaged an apartment complex in the city of Lubbock by ripping off the roof. The high amounts of moisture within the cloud bearing layer also allowed these storms to create heavy rainfall which caused flash flooding in the city of Lubbock.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous reports were received of flash flooding within the city of Lubbock from law enforcement and members of the public. An intense thunderstorm slowly moved from southeast to northwest across the city of Lubbock producing heavy rainfall. Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet sites in the city of Lubbock recorded over an inch of rainfall in less than 20 minutes.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Numerous thunderstorms developed along and ahead of a persistent MCS in East Texas during the afternoon of June 11th. Thunderstorms began training ahead of the MCS, and the overlapping segments of heavy rainfall resulted in scattered flash flooding across parts of Smith County and Harrison County. Hourly rainfall rates within this activity were estimated at nearly 3 inches per hour. The uptick in convective coverage and intensity was due to the thunderstorms training along a NW-SE oriented instability axis characterized by 1000-3000 J/kg MLCAPE, 2-2.25 inch precipitable water values, and 20-30 knots of southwesterly effective shear amid a variety of convergence boundaries analyzed across the region. As a result, flash flooding occurred in the more urban locations of Tyler in Smith County and near Marshall in Harrison County.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding reported with water covering the road on Highway 80 between Marshall and Hallsville.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the early to late evening hours on the 4th of June severe thunderstorms moved through the southwest to south central Texas Panhandle. The main supercell that moved in first from eastern New Mexico, quickly intensified in Deaf Smith County, where it briefly produced a weak tornado that overturned a couple of irrigation pivots. The storm then continued to produce ping pong ball to even an instance of baseball size hail as it moved into Randall County.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were some locations where three to five inches of moving water accumulated on the road. Other isolated spots had one to two inches. Ditches were full in several spots and fields were flooded.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mid-level shortwave trough moved over Texas and combined with an abnormally moist airmass to generate thunderstorms. These storms were very efficient rain producers dropping locally heavy rain that led to flash flooding. There were also a few severe thunderstorms.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Training of thunderstorms with intense rainfall rates produced a swath of 3-8 inches of rain across San Antonio. Several vehicles were swept off the Loop 410 access road into Beitel Creek. There were 11 fatalities in this creek and the surrounding area. Ten people were rescued from the water, and two others were able to get to safety on their own. Damage from the flooding totaled $23 million across Bexar County.

records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple reports of minor street flooding were received from Beaumont.

records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several roads were impassable in Beaumont including the feeder along Hwy 69, Cedar, the intersection of College and MLK, the underpass in Downtown Beaumont, Orleans, and the feeder of I-10 near Babe Zaharias.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms developed ahead of a cold front on the afternoon of June 8th and rapidly became severe. These thunderstorms gradually developed into disorganized lines of thunderstorms through the late afternoon and evening, while a discrete supercell in the western Oklahoma and Texas Panhandles produced 4 tornadoes. Otherwise, these thunderstorms produced wind gusts up to 80 mph, hail up to 2.25 inches in diameter, and heavy rain that led to localized flash flooding.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Fast moving flood waters covered County Road J just off HWY 60. Water was at least 6 to 8 inches deep.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the second/third week of June, South Texas experienced an active and dynamic weather pattern that led to several impactful weather events, including heavy rainfall, flash flooding, thunderstorm wind damage, a weak tornado, and a waterspout. The unsettled conditions were driven by a combination of deep tropical moisture, persistent upper-level disturbances, and an unstable atmosphere. PWATs frequently exceeded 2.0 inches (well above the climatological average) supporting efficient rainfall production. A series of MCSs and repeated rounds of convection produced widespread rainfall totals between 0.5-2.5 inches across much of the region, with localized amounts exceeding 9 inches, especially in the northeast Coastal Bend. These intense rainfall rates, coupled with slow-moving or training storms, resulted in significant flash flooding, prompting Flood Watches and multiple Flash Flood Warnings. The severe weather was not limited to flooding. Strong to severe thunderstorms also brought damaging winds, particularly across the Victoria Crossroads and Coastal Plains. Outflow boundaries from earlier storms helped initiate new rounds of convection, some of which strengthened rapidly in the presence of deep-layer shear and enhanced low-level inflow. This environment also proved favorable for brief, low-end tornadoes and waterspouts, with at least one weak tornado and a waterspout being reported during the active stretch.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Total rainfall accumulation of 3.82 inches.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered showers and thunderstorms developed during the early afternoon of July 9th across the Coastal Plains and Brush Country. This activity was due to a combination of factors: some atmospheric energy skirting the edge of a ridge in the Gulf, the arrival of the sea breeze, and abundant moisture in the region. records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Repeating bands of tropical rainfall impacted eastern Cameron and southern Willacy County during the daylight hours of July 1, with daily totals, most between 6 AM and 6 PM CST, averaging 3 inches or higher. Two longer-duration bands impacted southeast Cameron County during the late morning and late afternoon, with each producing minor but notable street flooding on South Padre Island and possibly Port Isabel.  Total measured and estimated rainfall was 5 to nearly 8 inches, highest between Laguna Vista and just west of Port Isabel.||Across the larger cities of Brownsville and Harlingen, total rainfall for the period was closer to 3-5 inches, with breaks between bands sufficient to keep water to ponding vs. street flooding.  A pocket of 5 to 7 inches fell in open fields in southwest Cameron, with no reports received.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: A social media video posted by KRGV-Channel 5 news showed 1 to 2 feet of water covering portions of Padre Blvd. in the City of South Padre Island, with some high water on side streets to the west, toward Laguna Madre Bay.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Several rounds of showers and thunderstorms pummeled the Lower Rio Grande Valley, especially during the afternoon and overnight hours of March 27th into early on March 28th, resulting in historic seasonal rainfall and widespread flash and areal flooding across the RGV.  Total rainfall ranged from 8 to nearly 19 inches based on trusted observations, with 10 inches or more falling across some of the highest populated locations from south McAllen through the south side of Interstate Highway 2 in Hidalgo County, then farther north in Cameron County, where 12 to nearly 19 inches fell between La Feria and Rio Hondo, including Harlingen and San Benito. Trusted radar estimates indicated up to 20.5 inches in east Harlingen, but as of this writing there were no verified values this high from trusted observers.||Initial rainfall began late on March 26th in eastern and southern Cameron County, with flooding in east Brownsville toward Port Isabel around sunrise on the 27th. ||Nearly five thousand homes and other structures were impacted, with more than two thousand having major damage or destruction due to 2 or more feet of water in them. Hundreds of local roads were flooded with up to 4 feet of water in some places, and at least one thousand vehicles trapped on flooded roads were damaged or totaled. Unfortunately, there were fatalities, with five dead on the U.S. side of the Rio Grande due to drowning and a lightning-induced fire, and one on the Mexican side of the border in Reynosa.||In addition to the flooding, wind damage occurred in several locations, with two small tornadoes touching down during the late afternoon of the 27th near Edcouch, and just after midnight on the 28th in Port Isabel.||Though damage estimates were still unknown as of late May, it is estimated that total damage was upwards of $100 million.  By early July, damage estimates had risen to $157 million; these numbers only included initial values of Public Assistance (PA) of $94 million, and $63 million in Individual Assistance in much of the Rio Grande Valley.  These values did not include privately-insured damage, and totals were likely to exceed $200 million. Additional damage estimates will be available by the end of 2025.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Torrential rains moved out from the McAllen/metro into the mid-Valley section of Hidalgo County, to include locations east of Edinburg, including Elsa/Edcouch, then south through San Juan, Alamo, and Donna, extending south to around Military Highway (US 281) east of Pharr and near the Rio Grande.||Poor drainage locations flooded with at least 3 feet of water depth, and nearly the entire IH-2 frontage road had 2 to 3 or more feet of water depth, with dozens of vehicles stranded and at least one hundred more removed from the floodwaters. A number of farm-to-market and state highways had pockets of flood waters, forcing closures that lasted into March 28th. ||In this flood area, there were three known drownings when vehicles became submerged in deeper waters in canals/drainage areas during encounters with law enforcement.  One drowning was a juvenile who was unable to be rescued from a vehicle that submerged near Edcouch.||Damage details and further information will be available later in 2025 from these areas.

records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Torrential rains that previously affected the McAllen/Edinburg metro area reached southeast Hidalgo County, from south of Weslaco to Edcouch and east to the Hidalgo/Cameron line, then south along the Mercedes/La Feria line and all the way to between Progreso and just west of Santa Maria. Similar to the situation in the Donna-Weslaco area, the IH-2 frontage road was littered with flooded vehicles, with rescued vehicles along the side of the elevated expressway.  An estimated 3 or more feet of water was on the frontage roads.||The rain in this area came in multiple rounds.  A first round occurred between 430 and 6 PM, with additional rounds between 7 and 8 PM and again fro 930 to around 11 PM,and a final windy round around midnight March 28th CST (1 AM CDT). Water rescues were first reported in Mercedes at around 7 PM CST (8 PM CDT).  As of this writing, damage was unknown but hundreds of structures likely had varying degrees, ranging from affected to major damage.   ||High water would continue well into March 28th and beyond; the flood control system (floodway) had up to 20% capacity due to spillage and pumping of urban flood areas into it. ||Full damage statistics will be available later in 2025.

records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant to locally devastating flash flooding began in the McAllen/Mission metropolitan area during mid-afternoon.  Rainfall rates of at least 3 in 30 minutes were too much for the city's drainage infrastructure to handle, and soon after, city fire/rescue/police reported  more than two dozen roads closed citywide and up to forty homes with an unknown amount of water depth inside, to the Emergency Management Coordinator. ||It was likely that several hundred homes had incident flooding, from affected to major damage - most concentrated in the south side of the city. Rainfall rates were historic for the season, ranging from 1/100 to 1/200 probability events (annual return frequency) over a 2-hour period. Cage Blvd. and E. Ferguson Ave., along/near the IH-69C frontage. records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Devastating and historic flash flooding occurred in northern and northeast portions of the Northwest Hill Country on July 4th with damage to many roads and houses. The combination of abundant tropical moisture associated with the remnants of Tropical Storm Barry and a weak upper level storm system, led to very slow moving or stationary thunderstorms producing very heavy and efficient rainfall. The heaviest rainfall amounts were 10 to 16 inches with localized rainfall totals of near 25 inches in northwest portions of Mason County.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Law enforcement reported that US Highway 87 was flooded near Dry Prong Road, north of the city of Mason. Time was estimated by radar.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Tropical Storm Barry moved into and dissipated over eastern Mexico. Moist air from the remnants of Barry moved northward into Texas. Precipitable water values over South-Central Texas increased to near record levels. A mid-level anticyclonic circulation developed and moved over Central Texas providing lift to generate thunderstorms. During the overnight period of July 3-4, a low-level jet streak set up over South Texas and led to training of thunderstorms over the Texas Hill Country. The combination of weather features generated efficient rain making storms that produced 2-3 inches of rain per hour for several hours over the headwaters of the Guadalupe River. Rainfall totals in the area were up to 11 inches which led to catastrophic and deadly flooding along the Guadalupe River in Kerr County. Heavy rain eventually moved eastward causing additional flooding. Flood water killed 117 people in Kerr County and caused an estimated $200 million in damage to public property and infrastructure. There was no estimate for private property damage. Kerr County officials estimated 2,000 structures were damaged or destroyed.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced 2-4 inches of rain sending water from the confluence of Kent Creek and the West Frio River over RM 336 approximately ten miles north of Leakey.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An MCS (which originated in southwestern Oklahoma and northern Texas) moved into the northern Permian Basin during the early morning hours of the 9th. Though the system was weakening as it moved into the Permian Basin, it was able to produce damaging winds in Snyder. Flash flooding and water rescues were also reported in Odessa due to heavy rain associated with the decaying MCS.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: A total of 12 water rescues were reported throughout the city of Odessa. The time of occurrence is estimated by radar. The cost of damages is also estimated.

When the water reached the bridge it was carrying a house that got stuck in the trees next to the bridge.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An upper level system coincided with abundant atmospheric moisture across the Texas Panhandle on the evening of the 24th. This resulted in scattered thunderstorms that eventually grew into widespread thunderstorm activity. A few storms became strong to severe thunderstorms that produced heavy rainfall, severe wind gusts, and a localized occurrence of hail up to ping pong ball size. The biggest hazard that occurred during this event was the flash flooding that occurred in the Amarillo and Canyon areas. records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Significant banding of heavy showers and thunderstorms with cell-training occurred on the morning of August 29th across East Texas and North Louisiana, posing the threat of flash flooding. A gradual increase in warm air advection and isentropic ascent was noted on the north side of a quasi-stationary frontal boundary and within a very moist and moderately unstable air mass. MUCAPE values ranged from 1000 to 2000 J/kg along the front from Deep East Texas into Central Louisiana. However, much of the elevated convection was rooted within the instability gradient farther north along the Arkansas/Louisiana border along with adjacent areas to the west and east. This was also where there was some modest frontogenesis and related forcing observed in the 925 to 850 millibar layer. In addition, precipitable water values were on the order of 2 to 2.25 inches and suggestive of a very tropical environment. The resulting heavy rain rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour led to numerous reports of flash flooding across parts of East Texas.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flooding reported with high water covering the roadway in Joaquin near the intersection of Highway 7 and FM Road 139. Flooding was also reported just west of this location  along Highway 84 in Joaquin.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Precipitable water values over South-Central Texas remained near record levels, and a mid-level anticyclonic circulation continued over Central Texas providing lift to generate thunderstorms. These storms were efficient rain making storms leading to another night of excessive rainfall. Parts of Burnet and Travis Counties received 12-16 inches of rain in approximately six hours that led to deadly flash flooding. Eighteen people died in flood waters: four in Burnet County, ten in Travis, and four in Williamson. The Travis County Emergency Manager estimated the cost of damage to public property and infrastructure at $5 million. The Burnet County Emergency Manager estimated the cost of damage to public property and infrastructure at $6 million. The Williamson County Emergency Manager estimated the cost of damage to public property and infrastructure at $25 million.

Walden Dr. prompted evacuations of the Georgetown Animal Shelter, VFW Post, Masonic Lodge, Holly Street Village, and the San Gabriel Crisis Center. The S. Austin Ave. bridge was closed. records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Slow-moving thunderstorms brought heavy rain  for several hours to Burnet on the morning of July 5. Burnet Municipal Airport reported 8.67 inches of rain. An LCRA gauge in Burnet reported 11.67 inches. The torrential rainfall caused the rapid rise of Hamilton Creek. Additional inundation also occurred along Daugherty Branch and Haynie Branch in Burnet. Homes, businesses, and other buildings along Hamilton Creek experienced up to 7 ft of inundation. Oak St. in the northwestern part of the city was especially hard hit by the swollen Hamilton Creek. Around a dozen homes along the road were damaged, primarily near 7th and 8th Street. One house was torn off its foundation and was carried by floodwaters onto the opposite side of the street. Several businesses were flooded along South Water St. A 57 year old man was swept by floodwaters while commuting through Burnet along US 281. His body was recovered about a quarter mile away from his vehicle along Hamilton Creek. Most of the units at the Hamilton Creek Manor housing complex were impacted by floodwaters. Fields at YMCA of the Highland Lakes on the south side of Burnet were damaged by flooding with fences washed out and dugouts damaged. Pafford Place Assisted Living was heavily damaged. An 85 year old man at the facility drowned in the flooding. Seven others were successfully evacuated from Pafford Place. Parts of Burnet Municipal Airport experienced 5 to 7 ft of inundation, resulting in damage to PAPI lighting and the runway. Several homes were inundated along Delaware Creek to the west and southwest of Burnet with washouts on roads. Across the county first responders rescued at least 63 people. The county Emergency Manager estimated more than 400 homes were affected and the damages were at least $6 million.

The heaviest rainfall amounts were 10 to 16 inches in northern San Angelo where the majority of the flash flooding occurred.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Tropical Storm Barry moved into and dissipated over eastern Mexico. Moist air from the remnants of Barry moved northward into Texas. Precipitable water values over South-Central Texas increased to near record levels. A mid-level anticyclonic circulation developed and moved over Central Texas providing lift to generate thunderstorms. During the overnight period of July 3-4, a low-level jet streak set up over South Texas and led to training of thunderstorms over the Texas Hill Country. The combination of weather features generated efficient rain making storms that produced 2-3 inches of rain per hour for several hours over the headwaters of the Guadalupe River. Rainfall totals in the area were up to 11 inches which led to catastrophic and deadly flooding along the Guadalupe River in Kerr County. Heavy rain eventually moved eastward causing additional flooding. Flood water killed 117 people in Kerr County and caused an estimated $200 million in damage to public property and infrastructure. There was no estimate for private property damage. Kerr County officials estimated 2,000 structures were damaged or destroyed.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: There was catastrophic and deadly flash flooding along the South Fork Guadalupe River after around ten inches of rain fell in approximately four hours. On Hwy 39 the debris started at the confluence of Mullen Creek and South Fork Guadalupe River. The South Fork Guadalupe River topped the Hwy 39 bridge west of Auld Rd. S. and the high-water mark was 23.77 feet above the river. Five feet of water damaged the bottom floor of the River Inn and Resort. There were large sections of the exterior walls removed by water. Water reached 7.5 feet in a house along Hwy 39 which destroyed the building. Water reached the Hunt Volunteer Fire Department station on Fisher Ranch Rd. 400 feet from the river. Heart O���the Hills Camp and many houses nearby were demolished. There was major damage to Crider���s Rodeo and Dance Hall. Several homes near Hwy 39 and Rustic Hill Rd. were wiped off their foundations. The Hunt Post Office and the Hunt Store were destroyed. The first floor of a house near the confluence of the North and South Fork flooded and the residents sheltered on the second floor. Another nearby house had only one floor, and the homeowner escaped and floated on a mattress until rescued by a helicopter. Debris damaged the Hwy 39 bridge over the river in Hunt. The river gage at Hunt was destroyed, and the USGS estimated the river crested at a record 37.51 feet. Sixty-one people died in the flood along this stretch of the river, and one was still missing. Twenty-seven of the fatalities were at Camp Mystic, a summer camp for girls, including the owner of the camp, two counselors, and 25 girls ages 8-10 years old. There were 12 fatalities at the Casa Bonita neighborhood where a number of homes were washed away. Most the other fatalities were in homes along the river that were washed away. One man had helped his family escape their house through a bedroom window, but was not able to make it out himself. One person was in a vehicle trying to escape the flood water, but was washed away. Across Kerr County damage to public property and infrastructure was estimated to be $200 million. There was no damage estimate for private property. County officials estimated 2,000 structures were damaged.

The flood wave moved downstream from Hunt to Kerrville. An NWS Flood Survey team found water in some houses along the Guadalupe downstream of Hunt reached eight feet. Numerous homes were flooded in the Bumble Bee Hills subdivision. Water reached as high as 5.5 feet in houses. The Cade Loop bridge over the Guadalupe was shifted by flood water. The guardrail and roadway of the Indian Creek Rd. bridge were damaged. The guardrail was torn away as were pieces of the roadway. Two RV parks and campgrounds in Ingram were wiped away by flood water. There were 46 people killed by flood waters, and one person was still missing. All of the fatalities along this stretch of the river were in the Ingram area and most of them were from the RV parks. One man died when he severed an artery breaking a window to help his family escape their flooded house. Across Kerr County damage to public property and infrastructure was estimated to be $200 million. There was no damage estimate for private property. records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mature linear thunderstorm complex developed across the Middle Red River Valley on November 24th and extended from Southwest Arkansas south-southwestward into East Texas and Northwest Louisiana. This thunderstorm complex was slow in its forward propagation eastward while producing areas of 0.5-1 inch/hour rain rates. An outflow boundary from this activity also extended farther westward from Longview to near Waco, Texas, where another well-organized linear complex moved eastward and also produced 0.5-1.5 inch/hour rain rates. In addition, heating along and south of a synoptic warm front across east Texas also aided in destabilization to support strengthening convection. This ultimately led to 2-4 inch rainfall totals across parts of East Texas and Northwest Louisiana, resulting in scattered instances of flash flooding, particularly where the greatest rainfall occurred over low-lying and urban areas. An isolated damaging wind report was also recorded with a downed tree near Nesbitt in Harrison County.

records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rain from slow-moving thunderstorms fell into the Hamilton Creek watershed contributing to a rapid rise of the creek that moved downstream near Marble Falls into the Colorado River. While only 1 to 2 inches of rain fell over Marble Falls, a swath of over 10 inches of rain occurred within the watershed upstream. An LCRA stream gauge on Hamilton Creek near Marble Falls measured a rise of 18.65 ft in about 90 minutes with 49,970 cfs before the gauge stopped reporting data. Widespread inundation and downing of trees occurred along the Hamilton Creek, with the extent of inundation at times nearly 1/3 mile across near FM 1431. The CR 341 crossing along Hamilton Creek was completely washed out on both approaches, leaving only a significantly damaged central concrete segment. The south approach to the CR 340/Mormon Hill Rd crossing was scoured out by floodwaters. Several homes were flooded along Hamilton Creek Rd. farther downstream of the CR 341 crossing. The Cedar Stays RV Park, located along the creek near FM 1431, saw major impacts. About 50 RVs were parked there overnight. All RVs were impacted by flooding and most were total losses. RVs closest to the creek experienced nearly 10 ft of inundation. RVs and other vehicles were swept into trees and the surrounding vegetation. Residents awoke to water entering their vehicles and climbed atop their RVs and the roof of the RV park office to avoid floodwaters and be rescued. Helicopters and boats were dispatched to aid water rescues. A 79-year-old male resident of the park died in the flooding. Hamilton Creek floodwaters overtopped the FM 1431 bridge, damaging the guardrail and washing out part of the crossing.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A heavy rainfall event across South Texas developed as a strong upper-level trough extended southward from the Great Lakes into Texas, providing large-scale ascent and enhanced positive vorticity advection. At the surface, a cold front pushed into the region and eventually stalled, serving as the main focus for lift while interacting with outflow boundaries from earlier convection. Ahead of the front, deep Gulf moisture surged northward with PWATs climbing to near or above the 99th percentile for early fall, creating an environment highly favorable for efficient rainfall production. Instability was plentiful, with CAPE values exceeding 2500 J/kg, supporting thunderstorm development, while modest shear allowed for organized clusters. Initially, convection initiated along prefrontal boundaries and central Texas storms drifting south, producing locally strong winds, but as storms slowed overnight, the primary threat shifted to hydrology. Slow-moving and training cells, fueled by abundant instability and anomalous moisture, wrung out widespread 1���2 inches of rainfall with localized amounts of 3���4 inches. This combination of deep tropical moisture, frontal convergence, upper-level support, and storm interactions ultimately produced the widespread heavy rain and scattered flooding concerns across the region--primarily in Laredo/Webb County.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Total of 3.15 inches.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stalled surface boundary and weak upper level disturbance worked together to form severe storms over the northwest to central Texas Panhandle. A strongly unstable atmosphere along with favorable wind shear was in place, which supported strong damaging winds and very large hail from thunderstorms that developed. Storms developed over the central Texas Panhandle and initially produced small hail and heavy rain, but a few storms grew stronger and produced damaging winds that resulted in some downed power poles. Another later round of storms affected the far northwest Texas Panhandle and produced hail up to tennis ball size and 70mph wind gusts.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: A road northwest of Washburn was flooded with an estimated two to three feet of standing water across it.  A truck was stalled in the water and lawns and driveways had water ponded on them.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A line of strong to severe thunderstorms developed over Corpus Christi area from a weak shortwave trough and shifted southward into Deep South Texas. As the storms ran into very unstable air across the Rio Grande Valley, they formed into a cluster and become locally severe.  Several microbursts and some hail (unknown size) were generated from the cluster, including a several-mile track between North Alamo and Donna/Weslaco, on June 12th, 2025. ||The microburst resulted in isolated to scattered structural damage to roofs, traffic lights, fences, trailers, power poles, as well as trees. There were no known injuries. Two to potentially three inches of rain in the McAllen metropolitan area resulted in urban flooding for around 2 hours there.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: The San Antonio Express-News reported, via video reports on social media, urban flooding with water depths up to 2 feet in streets across portions of the McAllen metropolitan region during the early to mid evening. Rainfall totals ranged from 2.5 to nearly 3 inches, much which fell within 90 to 120 minutes.  ||Damage to vehicles was unknown, though several had water levels halfway to two-thirds the way up their tire heights.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The atmosphere on September 7th remained well saturated, with PWAT values into the 1.9 to 2.2 inch range. This deep moisture combined with the passage of a frontal boundary that extended along the coast and continued to move offshore during the early morning hours produced periods of heavy rainfall across South Texas. records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: A total of 3.05 inches of rain measured between 1:00PM-4:40PM.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A trough to the west, coupled with the effects of moist upslope flow, helped trigger scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms across far West Texas and Southeast New Mexico throughout the day on September 28th. records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: A delayed report was received of flash flooding between the Buffalo Trail Boy Scout Camp and State Highway 17. Roads leading into the camp were reported to be impassible, especially at low water crossings. The camp itself did not flood. The time of occurrence is  partially estimated from radar. No damage was reported.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combination of a strong upper level area of low pressure and a cold front resulted in numerous severe thunderstorms across the Big Country during the late afternoon and night time hours. Also, extreme surface instability and strong wind shear helped produce supercell thunderstorms and significant severe weather. The severe storms produced very large hail and intense damaging winds including significant wind damage at the KTXS television studio in Abilene, Texas and a swath of damaging winds from a downburst in Fisher County. The strongest wind speeds ranged from 85 to 100 mph with some of these severe storms.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of flood waters over FM 605 and FM 707 on social media. Some portions of the road had flood water depth around 2 feet. Estimated time of peak flooding based on radar data.

records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding. Two and half inches of rain fell in Eagle Pass, which led to flooding at the intersection of Royal Point Dr. and Royal Ridge Dr. A person was rescued from a car stranded in the flood water.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A small but potent slow-moving thunderstorm dropped rainfall rates of 2 inches per hour for about 2 hours in a small area between Olmito and Rancho Viejo, about 11 miles north-northwest of downtown Brownsville. records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An isolated thunderstorm initially developed over northwestern Hale County and drifted to the southeast over Hale Center (Hale County). records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Local broadcast media relayed a video of flooding on Interstate-27 at the Cleveland Street underpass in Hale Center. The video also showed numerous vehicles stranded in flooded waters on the Interstate Highway.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A heavy rainfall event across South Texas developed as a strong upper-level trough extended southward from the Great Lakes into Texas, providing large-scale ascent and enhanced positive vorticity advection. At the surface, a cold front pushed into the region and eventually stalled, serving as the main focus for lift while interacting with outflow boundaries from earlier convection. Ahead of the front, deep Gulf moisture surged northward with PWATs climbing to near or above the 99th percentile for early fall, creating an environment highly favorable for efficient rainfall production. Instability was plentiful, with CAPE values exceeding 2500 J/kg, supporting thunderstorm development, while modest shear allowed for organized clusters. Initially, convection initiated along prefrontal boundaries and central Texas storms drifting south, producing locally strong winds, but as storms slowed overnight, the primary threat shifted to hydrology. Slow-moving and training cells, fueled by abundant instability and anomalous moisture, wrung out widespread 1���2 inches of rainfall with localized amounts of 3���4 inches. This combination of deep tropical moisture, frontal convergence, upper-level support, and storm interactions ultimately produced the widespread heavy rain and scattered flooding concerns across the region--primarily in Laredo/Webb County.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Numerous streets flooded on south side of Laredo.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the evening of September 9th, a very subtle upper level system passed over the region, which allowed several thunderstorms to develop across the western to central Texas Panhandle. The atmosphere was strongly unstable for September standards, combined with moderate wind shear and high moisture content, and this proved to be conducive for storms to produce severe hail, winds, and localized flooding. A few severe wind gusts were observed with two of the strongest storms, the highest of which were 70 mph occurring at the NWS Amarillo office and another northeast of Palo Duro Canyon in Armstrong County. Most hail was sub-severe, but quarter sized hail was observed with a severe storm in Carson County.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Highway 207 between Conway and Claude was closed due to three feet of water over the  highway.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak cold front extended from Eastern Oklahoma into Northeast Texas during the late evening into the early morning hours of January 9th-10th, and separated a warm, moist, and unstable air mass to its east, with a slightly cooler but drier air mass to the west. A surface low developed during the evening and overnight hours along the frontal boundary, enhancing a deep southerly low level flow into East Texas and North Louisiana, with a longwave trough shifting east through the Rockies into the Southern Plains enhancing large scale forcing along and ahead of the front across the warm sector. Thus, scattered to numerous showers and thunderstorms developed across this area, some of which produced locally heavy rainfall in the city of Tyler in Smith County Texas. Localized flash flooding was observed here where high water covered Loop 323 near Troup Highway and University Street, before the storms shifted east into Northwest Louisiana shortly after midnight and produced insolated instances of severe weather.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: High water covered Loop 323 near Troup Highway and University Street in Tyler.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An approaching upper-level trough interacted with anomalously high moisture across west Texas, resulting in shower and thunderstorm development that afternoon and evening. Initially isolated to scattered showers and storms eventually intensified and coalesced into a broken line as they moved across the Permian Basin. Large hail was reported near Monahans before the line developed. Heavy rain also led to flash flooding in the Midland/Odessa area. Additional convection developed later that night, but no additional severe reports were received.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A compact but strong upper level short wave trough tracked across Baja California on the afternoon of the 13th. Large scale ascent from an upper level jet streak interacted with abundant moisture streaming overhead at mid and upper levels of the atmosphere. Low level moisture streaming into the region combined with warm surface temperatures creating an unstable atmosphere by late afternoon. This resulted in scattered thunderstorms from late in the afternoon through the evening hours of the 13th. One of these storms produced severe winds near Slaton (Lubbock County). The abundant amount of moisture in the atmosphere also was able to produce heavy rainfall and flash flooding within the city of Lubbock (Lubbock County). Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet sites measured rainfall rates as high as four inches per hour.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: A cluster of mostly non-severe thunderstorms moved over the city of Lubbock early in the evening of the 13th. Abundant amounts of moisture in the atmosphere allowed for these storms to produce heavy rainfall over a short period of time. Several Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet sites within the city of Lubbock measured instantaneous rainfall rates of up to four inches per hour. These intense rainfall rates caused flash flooding on city streets for a brief period of time.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A persistent and highly moisture-laden tropical pattern set the stage for the flash flooding event from June 19-21. Thunderstorms initially developed along the Sierra Madre Oriental and crossed into South Texas on June 19, encountering an environment characterized by extremely high precipitable water values of 2.2-2.5+ inches, extreme instability with CAPE often exceeding 2,500-4,500 J/kg, and weak steering winds. As a stubborn upper-level closed low became established over South Texas, deep tropical moisture continued streaming inland on persistent southeast to east onshore flow. Multiple outflow boundaries, a mid-level vorticity maximum, and the sea breeze provided repeated lifting mechanisms for thunderstorm development. With storm motions generally under 10-15 kt and low-level inflow often stronger than the steering flow, thunderstorms repeatedly back-built, trained, and regenerated over the same locations. Rainfall rates of 2-3+ inches per hour became common, while saturated soils from prior heavy rainfall further reduced infiltration capacity. The combination of near-record atmospheric moisture, slow-moving and training thunderstorms, and several rounds of convection associated with the stationary upper low ultimately led to widespread flash flooding concerns across South Texas and the Coastal Bend through June 21.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Hot temperatures on the afternoon of the 11th slowed down a cold front moving through the area but also provided a focus for thunderstorm development. Strong instability, resulting from the warm temperatures and high moisture, ahead of the front fueled the rapid development of severe thunderstorms from the late afternoon into the evening hours. Thunderstorms initially developed over the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle and northern Rolling Plains where temperatures in excess of 100 degrees allowed updrafts to break through a capping inversion. Atmospheric flow was weak which allowed storms to move slowly and create torrential rainfall in some locations. Some roads within the city of Levelland (Hockley County) became impassable because of water over the road. The most significant thunderstorm developed over southern Lubbock County and moved southward producing severe wind gusts and wind damage throughout Lynn County. These winds caused minor but widespread damage throughout the towns of Tahoka and Wilson.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: A nearly stationary storm over the city of Levelland created heavy rainfall leading to excessive runoff. A report was received that portions of Texas Highway 114 were impassable within the city of Levelland.

Synoptic lift ahead of this feature, coupled with upslope flow and some lift from decaying outflow, allowed showers and thunderstorms to develop in/around the higher terrain and in western portions of the Permian Basin. Convection tended to move slowly and produce heavy rainfall during the evening and into the early morning hours of the 5th. As a result, flash flooding was reported in Gaines and Pecos Counties.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A significant flash flooding event began across South Texas on June 15, 2026 as an exceptionally moist tropical air mass overspread the region ahead of a slow-moving frontal boundary and an upper-level disturbance lifting out of northern Mexico. Deep tropical moisture associated with the remnants of former Tropical Storm Cristina and a developing low-pressure area near the Texas coast pushed precipitable water values into the 2.3-2.7 inch range, near or above daily record levels and roughly three standard deviations above normal for mid-June. At the same time, abundant instability, saturated atmospheric profiles, and deep warm cloud layers supported highly efficient rainfall production, with rainfall rates frequently reaching 2-4 inches per hour and locally approaching 5 inches per hour. A slow-moving mesoscale convective system that had developed farther north sagged southward into South Texas while repeated bands of thunderstorms trained over the same locations along the frontal boundary and zones of strong low-level moisture convergence. Weak steering currents and persistent inflow from the Gulf allowed storms to repeatedly redevelop over affected areas, producing localized rainfall totals of 3-5 inches in only a few hours and ultimately widespread totals of 4-8 inches. The combination of extreme rainfall rates, repeated training convection, and prolonged moisture transport resulted in dangerous flash flooding across portions of the Coastal Plains, Coastal Bend, Rio Grande Valley, and surrounding areas.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: High pressure over New Mexico helped trigger new storms off the higher terrain. These storms then moved to the south and east into the combined Panhandles. With favorable instability and wind shear, these storms became strong to severe with the main hazards being large hail and damaging winds. There were some supercells that did produce tornadoes across portions of the eastern combined Panhandles as well as high end wind damage from straight line winds. Given sufficient moisture in place, slow moving storms or storms that moved over the same locations, a few communities in the eastern combined Panhandles did receive heavy rainfall that resulted in flash flooding.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall and storms moving over the same locations brought flooding to Wheeler. Water flooded streets with around three to six inches deep in some locations. Water entered a nursing home with fire department having to move residents. Several roads in town and around town were impassable due to flooding including County roads 17 through 20 east of town.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak surface frontal boundary stalled out over portions of Deep East Texas, Lower Toledo Bend Country, and into North-central and Northeast Louisiana during the early morning hours on June 20th, separating warm and very moist air near and south of the front from the slightly drier air to the north. A weak upper level disturbance traversed east atop the front throughout the morning through the early afternoon hours, which enhanced large scale forcing for the development of showers and thunderstorms containing heavy rainfall. As this continued through the morning, the periods of heavy rain moved repeatedly over the same areas, which resulted in widespread amounts of 2-6+ inches falling over Southern Cherokee County Texas, as well as other portions of Deep East Texas, Central and Northeast Louisiana. ||Although no flooding was officially reported, here are storm total rainfall amounts that were measured from various stations in Southern Cherokee County: ||7 miles southwest of Alto: 6.06 inches (HADS gauge along Highway 21 southwest of Alto along the Neches River at the Houston County line).|6 miles west of Alto: 6.01 inches (Located just off CR 2325 near Highway 294).
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: The HADS gauge along Highway 21 southwest of Alto along the Neches River at the Houston County line measured a storm total of 6.06 inches.

Deep tropical moisture associated with the remnants of former Tropical Storm Cristina and a developing low-pressure area near the Texas coast pushed precipitable water values into the 2.3-2.7 inch range, near or above daily record levels and roughly three standard deviations above normal for mid-June. At the same time, abundant instability, saturated atmospheric profiles, and deep warm cloud layers supported highly efficient rainfall production, with rainfall rates frequently reaching 2-4 inches per hour and locally approaching 5 inches per hour. A slow-moving mesoscale convective system that had developed farther north sagged southward into South Texas while repeated bands of thunderstorms trained over the same locations along the frontal boundary and zones of strong low-level moisture convergence. Weak steering currents and persistent inflow from the Gulf allowed storms to repeatedly redevelop over affected areas, producing localized rainfall totals of 3-5 inches in only a few hours and ultimately widespread totals of 4-8 inches. The combination of extreme rainfall rates, repeated training convection, and prolonged moisture transport resulted in dangerous flash flooding across portions of the Coastal Plains, Coastal Bend, Rio Grande Valley, and surrounding areas.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak dryline formed during the day of the 30th and mixed eastward to the edge of the caprock. Convergence along the dryline, a weak short wave trough, and very hot temperatures contributed to convective initiation by mid-afternoon across the extreme southeastern Texas Panhandle and northern Rolling Plains. Storms repeatedly trained over Hall County producing intermittent severe winds gusts near Lesley (Hall County) for over an hour. Late in the afternoon additional thunderstorms developed in eastern New Mexico in the drier air and moved eastward into the South Plains. A very dry sub cloud layer allowed these storms to produce several severe wind gusts as they marched eastward towards the Interstate 27/US Highway 87 corridor. By the time storms reached Lubbock County late in the evening, they were moving very slowly which produced heavy rainfall over the city of Lubbock (Lubbock County). Numerous city roads on the south side of the city of Lubbock were inundated with water.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: A slow moving complex of thunderstorms moved over the city of Lubbock late in the evening on the 30th. Rain fall across the city of Lubbock was on the order of up to two inches per hour over a short time frame. Several reports were received of standing water over numerous roads throughout the southern portion of the city.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Widespread thunderstorms initially developed across the higher terrain of eastern New Mexico on the afternoon of the second, fueled by abundant moisture and aided by a mid-level disturbance moving across the region. The slow-moving thunderstorms ingested deep and rich moisture, leading to widespread moderate to heavy rainfall. The large expanse of rain gradually built eastward across the Texas/New Mexico state line and into the western South Plains and Texas Panhandle through the evening hours. Additional storm development blossomed along a low-level boundary over parts of the central and southeastern South Plains late in the evening, before being overtaken by the initial activity to the west early in the morning on the third. Relatively weak vertical wind shear and modest instability limited overall storm strength but produced torrential rainfall. Where the heaviest rain fell, portions of Farm to Market Road 212 and US Highway 380 in eastern and northeastern Lynn County were flooded. Flooding was also observed in and around Brownfield (Terry County), as well over northwestern portions of Cochran County, including in some locations along Farm to Market Road 596 northwest of Morton (Cochran County).
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS storm survey revealed extensive flooding in eastern Lynn County from heavy rainfall late on the third into the early morning hours of the fourth. The most widespread flooding occurred along Farm to Market Road 212 north of US Highway 380. Standing water still covered parts of the roadway the next morning. There also existed further evidence that water covered a greater portion of the roadway by the mud left behind as the water receded. Additional flooding occurred along US Highway 380 between Farm to Market 212 and Tahoka.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Late on the night of June 18, coverage of showers and thunderstorms expanded in association with a cold front and a slow-moving shortwave trough. This system then pushed south through North Texas early the morning of June 19. As the front continued southward and the shortwave propagated eastward, a second round of showers and storms developed across Central Texas on Saturday, June 20. The primary hazard accompanying these storms was flash flooding, though a few instances of damaging winds were also reported.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Showers and thunderstorms initially developed off the higher terrain in west Texas and southeast New Mexico during the afternoon of June 2nd. Later that evening, storms coalesced into a line behind an outflow boundary, which moved out of southeast New Mexico and into the Permian Basin. Severe winds accompanied this line as it moved across SE New Mexico and the western Basin. Heavy rainfall also led to instances of flash flooding through the morning of the 3rd before the line fully dissipated.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Video from Terlingua Fire Department showed water overflowing the banks of one of the  creeks near Terlingua. The total time of occurrence is estimated from radar and from the time of the initial report. No damage was reported.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Rich moisture advected into the region ahead of a dryline positioned across the south-central Texas Panhandle into the southwestern South Plains. Strong heating ahead of the dryline and a weak short wave trough aloft allowed scattered thunderstorms to develop across the central South Plains. A well mixed boundary layer allowed for storms to be high based and produce strong wind gusts. One Texas Tech University West Texas mesonet site near Abernathy (Hale County) recorded severe wind gusts with the outflow well ahead of the parent thunderstorm. Weak flow allowed for storms to have little to no movement which produced heavy rainfall and flash flooding in Hockley County.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms trained over southern and central Hockley County for several hours producing heavy rainfall. An emergency management official reported that portions of US Highway 385 were underwater from Farm to Market Road 41 through Farm to Market Road 1585.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The combined Panhandles were located between low pressure to the north and high pressure to the south. This allowed for late afternoon and evening storms to move from northwest to southeast across the region in a warm, moist and unstable environment. Supercell and multicell clusters of storms developed and affected the central and eastern portions of the Texas Panhandle during the later afternoon and evening hours. Large hail, damaging winds and flooding occurred across the region.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: High water made the intersection of FM2741  and County Road D impassible.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A persistent and highly moisture-laden tropical pattern set the stage for the flash flooding event from June 19-21. Thunderstorms initially developed along the Sierra Madre Oriental and crossed into South Texas on June 19, encountering an environment characterized by extremely high precipitable water values of 2.2-2.5+ inches, extreme instability with CAPE often exceeding 2,500-4,500 J/kg, and weak steering winds. As a stubborn upper-level closed low became established over South Texas, deep tropical moisture continued streaming inland on persistent southeast to east onshore flow. Multiple outflow boundaries, a mid-level vorticity maximum, and the sea breeze provided repeated lifting mechanisms for thunderstorm development. With storm motions generally under 10-15 kt and low-level inflow often stronger than the steering flow, thunderstorms repeatedly back-built, trained, and regenerated over the same locations. Rainfall rates of 2-3+ inches per hour became common, while saturated soils from prior heavy rainfall further reduced infiltration capacity. The combination of near-record atmospheric moisture, slow-moving and training thunderstorms, and several rounds of convection associated with the stationary upper low ultimately led to widespread flash flooding concerns across South Texas and the Coastal Bend through June 21.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Laredo PD reported that the intersection of Ejido and Potomac was closed due to  flooding. Time estimated from radar.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: During the afternoon of the 4th, an upper-level trough was moving in from the west. Synoptic lift ahead of this feature, coupled with upslope flow and some lift from decaying outflow, allowed showers and thunderstorms to develop in/around the higher terrain and in western portions of the Permian Basin. Convection tended to move slowly and produce heavy rainfall during the evening and into the early morning hours of the 5th. As a result, flash flooding was reported in Gaines and Pecos Counties.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A few hours after convection from the morning largely decayed, additional showers and thunderstorms developed thanks to an upper-level trough moving over west Texas and southeast New Mexico (along with upslope flow and some remnant outflow boundaries). records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: A member of the public reported water flowing over the intersection of West Highway 180 and County Road H. The total time of occurrence is estimated from radar. No damage was reported.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Based on SPC outlooks, mesoscale discussions, and local forecasts, the severe wind event during the early morning hours of May 27, 2026, was the result of a well-organized mesoscale convective system (MCS) that evolved from thunderstorms developing across West Texas on May 26. A weak but progressive mid-level shortwave trough moved eastward across Texas while a deepening surface low near the Big Bend maintained rich Gulf moisture with dewpoints in the upper 60s to lower 70s. Daytime heating combined with steep mid-level lapse rates produced moderate to strong instability, with MLCAPE generally ranging from 2,000 to 3,000 J/kg. Initial discrete supercells merged into a larger convective complex. As the storms organized into a line and interacted with additional convection over northern Mexico, a robust cold pool developed and strengthened. SPC discussions highlighted the formation of a rear-inflow jet and a bowing MCS, both classic indicators of an increasing damaging wind threat. By evening and overnight, the system was moving east-southeast into South Texas along an instability gradient, supported by 35-40 kt of deep-layer shear and abundant moisture. We noted that the reinforcing cold pool, strong nocturnal instability near 2,500 J/kg, and progressive MCS structure would make damaging winds the primary hazard. As the line approached the Coastal Plains and Middle Texas Coast during the predawn hours of May 27, SPC identified a corridor favorable for 60-70 mph wind gusts, with gust-front-orthogonal shear, a well-established cold pool, and forward-propagating storm clusters allowing the severe wind threat to persist all the way to the coast. Flash flooding also occurred with this system.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Vehicles reported stranded in flood waters near I-37 and McBride Lane.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe wind event across South Texas developed as a mid-level shortwave trough moved east from northern Mexico into West Texas, providing large-scale ascent and supporting widespread thunderstorm development. A moist and unstable air mass was already in place south of a quasi-stationary front, with surface dewpoints in the mid to upper 60s and moderate to strong instability ranging from 1,000-2,500 J/kg initially and later increasing to 3,000-4,000 J/kg across parts of South Texas. Enhanced wind shear of 30-40 knots, produced by strong westerly mid- and upper-level flow over weak easterly low-level winds, supported organized thunderstorm structures and the development of a nocturnal MCS moving out of Mexico. As the convectively enhanced shortwave crossed the region overnight, thunderstorms were able to maintain intensity and organize into clusters capable of producing strong outflow winds. Although relatively weak low-level lapse rates limited the overall severe wind threat, the combination of abundant moisture, extreme instability, and the potential for a strengthening cold pool within the MCS allowed water-loaded downbursts and pockets of damaging straight-line winds to develop as the system propagated east across South Texas during the early morning hours of May 21. Isolated flash flooding also occurred.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reports of numerous roads flooded with stranded vehicles on the south side of town.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Difluence ahead of an incoming shortwave interacted with ample moisture across west Texas and southeast New Mexico, allowing for showers and thunderstorms to develop across the area during the morning of the 26th. Later that evening, storms redeveloped in southeast New Mexico and moved into portions of west Texas. Large hail and strong winds were observed with these storms.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Public report of street flooding at the intersection of Hwy 158 and I-20. The total time of occurrence is partially estimated from radar. No damage was reported.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Storms moved through SE Texas and produced strong winds and heavy rainfall.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding was reported over portions of northeast Brazoria county. In the video, extensive inundation can be seen across two residential properties with both homes surrounded by water. One property had water over the front porch, reaching the front door. Flash flooding onset was estimated from gauge and radar observations. Another video shared by storm chasers showed other lawns and turf inundated with water, though inundation only seemed to reach the edges of these roadways.

records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding closing at least eight roads in western Comal County.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very hot temperatures and a dryline allowed scattered thunderstorms to develop on the afternoon of the 31st. Thunderstorms initially developed along this dryline from the northern Rolling Plains into the southern South Plains. The thunderstorms gradually grew upscale into a broken, slow moving line that persisted over the central Rolling Plains into the south-central South Plains through the evening hours. These slow moving thunderstorms primarily produced torrential rainfall but also large hail and damaging wind gusts. Excessive runoff from the prolonged heavy rain flooded fields and inundated area roadways. Some of the heaviest rainfall was along US Highway 87 north of Tahoka in Lynn County. Water over the roadway and a water rescue prompted the closure of the highway. Several additional vehicles became flooded out along US Highway 87. Additional flooding occurred along US Highway 380 west of Post (Garza County) and in northwestern Lubbock (Lubbock County). As storms decreased in intensity late in the evening, a couple of wake lows formed producing severe wind gusts near Slaton (Lubbock County) and Paducah (Cottle County).
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms continuously grew upscale along US Highway 380 in Garza County west of Post. On the evening of the 31st, law enforcement in Garza County reported flooding along US Highway 380 near Farm to Market Road 399. An NWS storm survey revealed portions of area roadways previously had water running over them as evidenced by mud on the road.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An incoming shortwave trough brought showers and some thunderstorms to west Texas and southeast New Mexico overnight April 30th and especially during the morning of May 1st. During the morning of the 1st, rainfall became locally heavy at times, which resulting in flash flooding in urban and low-lying areas. Showers largely cleared the area during the afternoon of the 1st as the shortwave moved east of MAF's CWA, taking the best lift and moisture with it.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: A web camera (operated by broadcast media) showed flash flooding of a low-water crossing in Andrews. The total time of occurrence is estimated by radar. No damage was reported.

Although the majority of these storms remained sub-severe, a few produced large hail. Additionally, the slow progression of the system led to heavy rainfall and flash flooding in some areas.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Emergency Manager reported the closure of Sachse Rd at Country Club Rd due to high  water.

records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: There were flooded roads in Irion County.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite dense cloud cover throughout the day, a couple of thunderstorms managed to develop during the evening of the 29th in the southeastern Permian Basin and Lower Trans-Pecos. On the 29th, storms were mainly across the southern TX Panhandle.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: A creek had water outside of its banks and an estimated one to two feet of water was over a dirt road.  The water appears to be up to a maintained road. This flooding occurred about four hours after the rain ended.

records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding. Flooding was reported throughout the city of Granite Shoals.

These sources of lift allowed for thunderstorms to develop across the Western Low Rolling Plains and the eastern Permian Basin. These thunderstorms produced very large hail, up to the size of baseballs. Meanwhile, as the front swept through the area high winds were recorded at a couple of Mesonet sites in west Texas and southeast New Mexico.

The storms produced swaths of severe winds and some large hail. Locally heavy rain that led to some flash flooding mainly north of the Austin area and in the Hill Country.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed ahead of a dryline and cold front on the afternoon of the 22nd. Storms were initially transient and struggled to become organized due to a lack of deep layer shear across the region. However, numerous outflow boundary formed which initiated new convection and were able to take advantage of a moist and unstable atmosphere. Hail as large as tennis balls were observed in Hale County. The numerous outflow boundaries created enough shear to generate several landspout tornadoes across the area. None of the many landspout tornadoes caused any known damage. Additionally, merging storms in southeastern Hale County produced torrential rainfall which led to flash flooding of roads and fields north of Petersburg.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Two supercell thunderstorms merged in eastern Hale County and remained nearly stationary for an hour before moving off to the northeast. Very heavy rainfall was observed with this thunderstorm. After the storm had moved away from the area, a storm chaser reported rushing water over Farm to Market Road 37 northwest of Petersburg.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: The afternoon sea breeze, combined with a weak upper level disturbance approaching the Lower Texas Coast, triggered two bands of slow-moving thunderstorms that dropped more than 3 of rainfall in a short period of time. records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front extended along the I-20 corridor of East Texas and North Louisiana during the morning and afternoon hours of June 15th, with a warm, very moist, and unstable air mass present south of the front. In fact, the vertical extent of the deep layer moisture profile was the greatest on record for the calendar day, and provided the fuel needed as a weak upper level disturbance moving into the region from the west enhanced large scale forcing within this very moist air mass. As a result, clusters of showers and thunderstorms containing very heavy rainfall developed along and south of I-20, producing excessively heavy hourly rainfall amounts of 2-3+ inches per hour across portions of Lower East Texas and North Louisiana. Widespread rainfall amounts of 1-3 inches, with isolated higher amounts in excess of 5 inches were observed, falling over a brief period of time which resulted in flash flooding. 5.11 inches of rain was measured in Marshall in Central Harrison County from these storms.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Several cars were stalled in high water on King Street.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Scattered thunderstorms developed early in the morning on June 23rd within a zone of weak theta-e advection at 850 millibars, from Southwest Oklahoma into Northeast Texas. Rich boundary layer moisture as well as overall strong instability was in place across this region, along with effective deep-layer shear of 35-40 knots. Wind profiles indicated 850 millibar winds out of the south to southeast at around 25 knots, aiding in lift across the warm advection zone. As low-level winds veered and strengthened during the morning hours, forcing for ascent also increased. Slow-moving thunderstorms with heavy rainfall began to rapidly increase in this environment, even extending through the afternoon. Given the high precipitable water (PWAT) environment, localized strong downbursts also occurred with some of these storms. Widespread rainfall amounts of 3-6+ inches fell over portions of Northeast Texas during the morning, contributing to areas of flash flooding. Isolated severe thunderstorms also developed over these areas during the afternoon, with renewed flash flooding with additional rainfall amounts of 2-5+ inches falling. As a result, several reports of flash flooding were recorded across Northeast Texas along with a few damaging wind reports.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Spotter reported flooding over FM Road 125 near Linden.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front extended along the Red River Valley bordering Southeast Oklahoma, extreme Northeast Texas, and into Southwest Arkansas during the morning hours of June 19th, with a warm, very moist and unstable air mass present across East Texas along and south of the front. An upper level disturbance traversed atop the front during the morning and early afternoon hours, enhancing large scale forcing for the development of numerous showers and thunderstorms along and south of the front. Given the very moist air mass in place, these storms were very efficient rainfall producers, with widespread rainfall amounts of 2-5+ inches falling over Central and Northern Red River and Bowie Counties in Northeast Texas. These excessive rainfall amounts in a short period of time resulted in reports of flash flooding across these areas, particularly in the Detroit and Dekalb areas with multiple roads flooded and water entering homes.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Water entered several homes and buildings in Detroit. Report from mPING.
