records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite considerable cloud cover across East Texas ahead of a cold front, relatively modest surface heating was ongoing by late morning on April 4th. A very moist air mass characterized by dew points in the upper 60s to lower 70s preceded the front. This environment supported scattered thunderstorm development along and ahead of the cold front, further aided by being on the southern fringe of the stronger mid-level winds helping propel the front. Additionally, MLCAPE values increasing to 1500+ J/kg and 25-35 knots of effective shear supported marginally organized storms capable of wind damage, flash flooding, and isolated tornadoes. However, poor mid-level lapse rates and a linear mode limited hail potential. As a result, one severe thunderstorm with quasi-supercell structure produced a brief tornado near Lindale in Smith County while a separate cluster of thunderstorms led to isolated flash flooding in Longview in Gregg County.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Very hot temperatures and a dryline allowed scattered thunderstorms to develop on the afternoon of the 31st. Thunderstorms initially developed along this dryline from the northern Rolling Plains into the southern South Plains. The thunderstorms gradually grew upscale into a broken, slow moving line that persisted over the central Rolling Plains into the south-central South Plains through the evening hours. These slow moving thunderstorms primarily produced torrential rainfall but also large hail and damaging wind gusts. Excessive runoff from the prolonged heavy rain flooded fields and inundated area roadways. Some of the heaviest rainfall was along US Highway 87 north of Tahoka in Lynn County. Water over the roadway and a water rescue prompted the closure of the highway. Several additional vehicles became flooded out along US Highway 87. Additional flooding occurred along US Highway 380 west of Post (Garza County) and in northwestern Lubbock (Lubbock County). As storms decreased in intensity late in the evening, a couple of wake lows formed producing severe wind gusts near Slaton (Lubbock County) and Paducah (Cottle County).

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A severe wind event across South Texas developed as a mid-level shortwave trough moved east from northern Mexico into West Texas, providing large-scale ascent and supporting widespread thunderstorm development. A moist and unstable air mass was already in place south of a quasi-stationary front, with surface dewpoints in the mid to upper 60s and moderate to strong instability ranging from 1,000-2,500 J/kg initially and later increasing to 3,000-4,000 J/kg across parts of South Texas. Enhanced wind shear of 30-40 knots, produced by strong westerly mid- and upper-level flow over weak easterly low-level winds, supported organized thunderstorm structures and the development of a nocturnal MCS moving out of Mexico. As the convectively enhanced shortwave crossed the region overnight, thunderstorms were able to maintain intensity and organize into clusters capable of producing strong outflow winds. Although relatively weak low-level lapse rates limited the overall severe wind threat, the combination of abundant moisture, extreme instability, and the potential for a strengthening cold pool within the MCS allowed water-loaded downbursts and pockets of damaging straight-line winds to develop as the system propagated east across South Texas during the early morning hours of May 21. Isolated flash flooding also occurred.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Reports of North Ocean Drive flooded between Magnolia Beach and Indianola, but passable.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Based on SPC outlooks, mesoscale discussions, and local forecasts, the severe wind event during the early morning hours of May 27, 2026, was the result of a well-organized mesoscale convective system (MCS) that evolved from thunderstorms developing across West Texas on May 26. A weak but progressive mid-level shortwave trough moved eastward across Texas while a deepening surface low near the Big Bend maintained rich Gulf moisture with dewpoints in the upper 60s to lower 70s. Daytime heating combined with steep mid-level lapse rates produced moderate to strong instability, with MLCAPE generally ranging from 2,000 to 3,000 J/kg. Initial discrete supercells merged into a larger convective complex. As the storms organized into a line and interacted with additional convection over northern Mexico, a robust cold pool developed and strengthened. SPC discussions highlighted the formation of a rear-inflow jet and a bowing MCS, both classic indicators of an increasing damaging wind threat. By evening and overnight, the system was moving east-southeast into South Texas along an instability gradient, supported by 35-40 kt of deep-layer shear and abundant moisture. We noted that the reinforcing cold pool, strong nocturnal instability near 2,500 J/kg, and progressive MCS structure would make damaging winds the primary hazard. As the line approached the Coastal Plains and Middle Texas Coast during the predawn hours of May 27, SPC identified a corridor favorable for 60-70 mph wind gusts, with gust-front-orthogonal shear, a well-established cold pool, and forward-propagating storm clusters allowing the severe wind threat to persist all the way to the coast. Flash flooding also occurred with this system.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Moisture was high for mid July across the combined Panhandles with precipitable water values in the 90th percentile.  This would result in efficient rainfall occurring from any storm that developed during the afternoon and evening hours of July 12th. A weak upper level disturbance moved across the region, and coupled with heating and unstable atmosphere, was able to produce some showers and thunderstorms during the afternoon. Outflow boundaries also contributed to additional storm development, including one that formed across the city of Amarillo and persisted for a long time. This storm produced efficient heavy rainfall that resulted in significant flooding across downtown and the southern sections of the city. Additionally, damaging winds and even a landspout occurred during these storms.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: The collision of two outflow boundaries right over Amarillo created additional thunderstorms that produced efficient rainfall of likely two to three inch per hour rainfall rates. These storms did not move out of the area quickly and heavy rainfall resulted in widespread flash flooding, especially across portions of the southwest side of the city. Fast moving flood waters occurred across many streets and parking lots, some of which were anywhere from six to eight inches deep or even up to 12 inches deep. There were multiple to numerous impassable roads with swift flowing water across them and water up to the wheel wells of many cars and SUVs. Several vehicles were stalled and flooded on the roads. Water flooded into some structures. This included Amarillo Square Apartments, which had two feet of water inside ground floor apartment units. In addition, dumpsters were being moved by these fast moving flood waters in some residential areas.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: July 12th marked the beginning of multiple days of heavy rainfall that led to flash flooding across west Texas and southeast New Mexico. A slow-moving trough made its way towards the region from the east throughout the week, undercutting and displacing an upper-level ridge. This trough interacted with ample moisture across the area, producing showers and thunderstorms that produced heavy rainfall. On the 12th, flash flooding was mainly reported in Scurry County near Snyder.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weakening Mesoscale Convective System (MCS) moved southeast into Northeast Texas during the early morning hours of July 5th, along a weak upper level disturbance aloft that drifted southeast into East Texas in the northwest flow aloft. While these storms dissipated by daybreak, they produced a large outflow boundary that propagated southeast to near and south of the I-20 corridor by afternoon, with strong heating, ample low level moisture, and resultant instability contributing to additional scattered showers and thunderstorms across this area of East Texas by mid and late afternoon. Some of these storms did become severe, with reports of damaging winds, hail, and isolated instances of localized flash flooding, before weakening during the early evening.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: High water covered FM 828 at County Road 285, and also on Clemson Drive in Southeast  Tyler.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Warm temperatures combined with sufficient mid level moisture, wind energy, and an approaching weather disturbance to produce scattered showers and thunderstorms during the afternoon of July 1st, especially across portions of the southern Texas Panhandle. Some of these were able to become strong to severe with damaging winds being the primary hazard. Slow movement of storms along with efficient heavy rainfall allowed for some flash flooding to occur.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall, along with multiple rounds of thunderstorms moving across the same locations, led to flooding in Hedley. An estimated one to two feet of standing water was noted with water approaching a house.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On the afternoon of the 12th, numerous thunderstorm outflow boundaries collided across the South Plains of West Texas. A very unstable atmosphere allowed scattered thunderstorms to develop. Although most of these storms were non-severe, a few severe wind gusts did occur across Lubbock County. A wet microburst occurred south of Idalou (Lubbock County) which caused roof damage to a barn and mobile homes. One outflow boundary over Lubbock County was slow moving which generated slow moving thunderstorms. Localized areas of heavy rainfall occurred over northwestern portions of the city of Lubbock and the city of Slaton where multiple vehicles became stalled in flood waters.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: A slow moving outflow boundary allowed thunderstorms to train across northwestern portions of the city of Lubbock. Local law enforcement and trained spotters reported numerous stranded vehicles on city streets.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weak surface outflow boundary associated with overnight storms in Kansas moved through the combined Panhandles and stalled just to the south of Amarillo. This allowed for a late start to any diurnal showers and thunderstorms to occur across the region as drier air was in place, limiting storm development. As this drier air moved out of the region by late afternoon, another surface boundary was located around the Highway 60 corridor. This, along with the more southern boundary, was the focus for storm development. Storms developed during the late afternoon and some became strong to severe with hail and damaging winds being observed across portions of the Panhandle, especially in locations along and south of the Highway 60 corridor. These storms were also efficient rain-producers with heavy rainfall occurring that led to some flash flooding in the area.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Another weather disturbance moved through the combined Panhandles on July 5th. Showers and thunderstorms were able to develop during the evening hours, some moving in from the west. The combination of storms and residual outflow boundaries combined to initiate a more organized line of storms that moved through the Amarillo area. These storms were efficient at producing heavy rainfall, which led to some flooding issues of both poor drainage locations but also vulnerable flooding locations.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Heavy rainfall led to some flash flooding concerns in Amarillo. I-40 under South Washington Street was closed and traffic was being re-routed due to the flooding. Several cars were stuck in flood waters. Flood waters covered the grill of a sedan, so therefore was estimated to be at least three feet of water. Highway 87 leading to Fillmore Street was also closed due to flooding.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A slow moving upper level low lingered over the area during the day on the 18th which resulted in scattered showers and thunderstorms across the entire region. Strong heating during the afternoon provided the necessary instability for thunderstorm development. Wind shear was weak so thunderstorms struggled to become organized but a few were able to produce severe wind gusts. One landspout was observed near Lorenzo that remained over open fields. Additionally, the lack of wind shear led to slow movement of storms which produced localized heavy rainfall. Minor flooding was reported in the town of Matador (Motley County).
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: An NWS cooperative weather observer reported 2.20 inches of rainfall in less than one hour near Matador. At the same time, a public report was received of flooding in Matador.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Over the course of the weekend, a meandering front and an unseasonably strong upper trough triggered widespread showers and thunderstorms across the region. Heavy rain from training storms ultimately resulted in flash flooding, particularly affecting several Central Texas counties. A significant flood event occurred in and around Waco costing millions of dollars.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Broadcast media reported significant urban flash flooding near the intersection of Waco Drive and Lake Air Drive in Waco. Multiple cars were seen stranded in the photo, which was relayed from social media. Local Emergency Management reported approximately 60 persons were rescued or needed assistance to safety across the county.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper-level ridge moved over the northern Great Plains allowing a moist, tropical airmass to move over South-Central Texas. Precipitable water values increased to greater than 2.0 inches which were near or above the 95th percentile of climatological values for this part of July. Multiple rounds of excessive rainfall were triggered by mid-level disturbances around the southern periphery of the high and low-level outflow boundaries. This convection was aided by nocturnal low-level jet streaks which led to slow moving, back building thunderstorms. Most of South-Central Texas received more than two inches of rain. The greatest totals were over Uvalde and Kinney Counties where 20-30 inches occurred. Another local maximum of 15-20 inches was observed in central Kerr County. Ten to 15 inches were widespread from Del Rio to Hondo and northward to northeastern Edwards to western Gillespie Counties. Damage estimates were near $115 million across South-Central Texas.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Thunderstorms produced heavy rain that led to flash flooding on the Bexar/Comal County line. FM 1863 at Cibolo Creek was flooded and impassable.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front was convectively reinforced south across East Texas to just north of the I-20 corridor, as well as North Louisiana during the morning hours of July 13th, ahead of bands of showers and thunderstorms that developed and moved east along the front from North into East Texas. The morning storms produced heavy rainfall which led to localized flooding in Smith County before diminishing, although the presence of the surface boundary and a weak upper level disturbance extending from Eastern Texas across North Louisiana into the Tennessee Valley contributed to large scale forcing within a hot, moist, and unstable air mass for the development of additional showers and thunderstorms across these areas during the mid and late afternoon. Given the weak steering currents, these storms were slow moving, and produced very heavy rainfall in a short period of time, leading to instances of flash flooding across portions of East Texas and Northwest Louisiana. Rainfall totals of 1-3 inches, with isolated totals in excess of 6 inches, were observed before the storms diminished during the evening.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Commerce Street in Tyler was flooded.

Flooding impacted the Chula Vista, primarily due to rises on the Espantosa Slough. Some homes experienced significant damage along FM65. Up to 3ft of inundation was reported at one home, with one eyewitness reporting floodwaters rising from ankle to waist height within 15 minutes. Some livestock were lost.||Across Zavala County, damage to public infrastructure reached $1.518 million. Countywide, 474 homes were affected by flooding, including 27 classified as destroyed, 156 classified as sustaining major damage, and 127 classified as sustaining minor damage, and 164 otherwise affected.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A stationary front was convectively reinforced south across East Texas to just north of the I-20 corridor, as well as North Louisiana during the morning hours of July 13th, ahead of bands of showers and thunderstorms that developed and moved east along the front from North into East Texas. The morning storms produced heavy rainfall which led to localized flooding in Smith County before diminishing, although the presence of the surface boundary and a weak upper level disturbance extending from Eastern Texas across North Louisiana into the Tennessee Valley contributed to large scale forcing within a hot, moist, and unstable air mass for the development of additional showers and thunderstorms across these areas during the mid and late afternoon. Given the weak steering currents, these storms were slow moving, and produced very heavy rainfall in a short period of time, leading to instances of flash flooding across portions of East Texas and Northwest Louisiana. Rainfall totals of 1-3 inches, with isolated totals in excess of 6 inches, were observed before the storms diminished during the evening.

records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: After receiving 2-6 inches of rain on the 14th, the Boerne area had another 6-10 inches early on the 15th. This led to severe flooding in Boerne. Water rescues were reported, and neighborhoods were cut off by flooded roads. Boerne police responded to 109 calls for service, of which 36 were high-water calls including a boat rescue of a stranded SUV at Herff Rd. and River Rd. Swift-water rescue teams extracted three people trapped in vehicles, including two walkout rescues and one boat rescue. Two of the rescues occurred at the Herff Rd. and River Rd. intersection. Most calls for service were along River Rd. and Cibolo Creek, with a few in the I-10 corridor. The city of Boerne encouraged voluntary evacuations in the Lake Country, Shoreline Park, Heart of Boerne, Evergreen, Yoalana, and West San Antonio Avenue areas. Evacuations occurred in low-lying areas near Cibolo Creek, at homes and at an apartment complex. Evacuations were also carried out along Ranger Creek and near Boerne City Lake. One home in Ranger Creek was flooded with 3 feet of water. The rise on Cibolo Creek inundated the Main St. bridge and Herff Rd. intersections and flooded River Road Park. The Herff and River Rd. intersection was under 2-3 feet of water. River Road was closed in all directions. Damage to roads and bridges around the county was estimated at $3 million.

records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Torrential rain from several slow-moving thunderstorms occurred along US90 in Kinney County on the morning of July 16. Rainfall totals across US90 were estimated to be above 8 inches with localized totals around 15 inches.||The flooding in Kinney County was one of the most significant in recent memory. Countywide, 80 total homes were flooded or otherwise affected, concentrated mainly in Brackettville and Fort Clark Springs. Of the 80 homes, at least 8 sustained major damage and at least 18 sustained minor damage. Water intrusion was reported to some classrooms on the Brackett ISD campus. All highways, farm-to-market, and ranch-to-market roads in the area were closed due to flooding, including US90 on both sides of Brackettville. Flooding occurred along Las Moras Creek along US90 and Gove St. Several roads sustained damage, including asphalt loss or damaged culverts. Washouts occurred on US90 at Pinto Creek. Flooding on Pinto Creek scoured out underlying portions of the RM2804 bridge. Lift stations were flooded. Evacuations occurred in Brackettville and Fort Clark Springs.||Damage to public infrastructure in Kinney County amounted to $2.8 million.

records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Multiple areas in Kerrville were affected. The Guadalupe River, Town Creek, and Quinlan Creek all overflowed their banks and flooded significant portions of Kerrville). Numerous water rescues and evacuations were conducted through the morning of July 16. Rescues mainly involved extracting people from vehicles driven into high-water areas. Many residences were evacuated in flood prone areas with floodwaters threatening. There were more than about 50 different evacuations of residences and apartment complexes. There was more than $55 million in damage to homes and infrastructure within the Kerrville city limits according to the assistant city manager. In August, the Kerrville mayor stated that damage to city infrastructure was estimated at a little under $100 million. Around $30 million of the damage was to the city���s water treatment plant, sewage lift stations, roads, and bridges. The combined public and private damage was estimated at $150 million for the county. FEMA reported 623 homes affected by flooding, with 7 destroyed, 131 with major damage, 373 with minor damage, and 111 others affected in some way. The city received at least 820 flood damage reports. The bridge leading from Junction Hwy to the Arcadia Loop area was partly washed out along Goat Creek, with the collapse of a 15-ft segment of the bridge. Buildings were observed floating onto the Arcadia Loop bridge. Most of Town Creek Road was either washed away or covered with debris. Large portions of the River Trail at Louise Hays Park were destroyed, heavily damaged, or covered in debris.  The Kerr County courthouse���s basement had at least 3-4 feet of floodwater with the county judge later reporting an estimate of ���as much as seven feet of water��� in the courthouse basement.

records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Significant rainfall farther upstream within the Howard Draw watershed led to rapid riverine flooding along Howard Draw and downstream along the Pecos River in western Val Verde County. The Pecos River gauge at Pandale Crossing just downstream of the Howard Draw confluence registered a steep and significant rise on the evening of July 17, rising to a crest of 15.93ft (89,700cfs) in Major flood at 2115CST. This was the highest crest measured at that site since 1996.||A vehicle was swept by flooding into the Devils Draw near the confluence with Howard Draw north of Pandale on the evening of July 17, resulting in the death of one of the two occupants. The other was hospitalized with serious injuries. The Pecos River overtopped the Langtry Rd bridge at Pandale Crossing on the evening of July 17, contorting segments of the metal guardrails. Farther downstream, two kayakers were rescued on the morning of July 18 after they became stranded by the rapid rise of the lower Pecos River near Camp Canyon.

records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: The Uvalde area and Leona River watershed received some of the heaviest rainfall in South-Central Texas during the July 2026 flood event. Rounds of torrential rain occurred each morning between July 14 and July 16. The headwaters of the Leona River saw 20 to 30 inches of rain during a 3-day stretch. CoCoRaHS observers reported 10 to 15 inches in the Uvalde area. ||Uvalde was among the areas most impacted by the flooding. Some homes experienced 3ft of inundation. An estimated 300 to 500 residents were displaced by flooding in Uvalde. Numerous water rescues occurred throughout the flood event. On the morning of July 16, a vehicle was swept off US83 near CR400 north of Uvalde along the Leona River, resulting in one fatality. The driver had reportedly eluded law enforcement warnings not to proceed up the roadway. Mandatory evacuations were ordered for residents along the Leona River during the event with broader voluntary evacuation orders, leading to the evacuation of hundreds of people. At one point, there were at least 256 people in shelters.||Damage to roads was widespread. TX55 sustained significant damage at several points due to rises on the Nueces River, particularly between Indian Creek Rd and CR410. records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong upper-level ridge moved over the northern Great Plains allowing a moist, tropical airmass to move over South-Central Texas. Precipitable water values increased to greater than 2.0 inches which were near or above the 95th percentile of climatological values for this part of July. Multiple rounds of excessive rainfall were triggered by mid-level disturbances around the southern periphery of the high and low-level outflow boundaries. This convection was aided by nocturnal low-level jet streaks which led to slow moving, back building thunderstorms. Most of South-Central Texas received more than two inches of rain. The greatest totals were over Uvalde and Kinney Counties where 20-30 inches occurred. Another local maximum of 15-20 inches was observed in central Kerr County. Ten to 15 inches were widespread from Del Rio to Hondo and northward to northeastern Edwards to western Gillespie Counties. Damage estimates were near $115 million across South-Central Texas.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: The FM481 bridge over the Nueces River 9 mi southwest of Uvalde partially collapsed with a segment of the bridge entirely swept away, along with washouts on parts of FM481 approaching the bridge. The cost of bridge repairs exceeded $3 million. The exact date and time of the collapse is unknown but is assigned the time of maximum Nueces River flood height.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unusually strong and deep upper level disturbance lingered across the Mid-South and into Southwest Arkansas, Northwest Louisiana, and East Texas during the early morning hours of July 7th, as it remained wedged in between two upper level ridges over the Southern Rockies into the western sections of the Southern Plains, and over the Eastern Seaboard and Southeast United States. This trough had focused numerous severe thunderstorms across the region on July 6th, with multiple outflow boundaries from these storms, coupled with ample moisture, large scale forcing along the upper trough itself, and renewed daytime heating which yielded strong instability, focusing shower and thunderstorm development during the morning and afternoon hours on the 7th across East Texas and North Louisiana. Some of these storms became severe, producing damaging winds that downed trees, an isolated instance of large hail, as well as heavy rainfall that led to localized flash flooding in Smith County throughout the cities of Tyler and Lindale, before diminishing late in the day.
records.EVENT_NARRATIVE: Flash flooding reported near 5th Street and Front Street in Tyler.

records.EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An unusually strong and deep upper level disturbance lingered across the Mid-South and into Southwest Arkansas, Northwest Louisiana, and East Texas during the early morning hours of July 7th, as it remained wedged in between two upper level ridges over the Southern Rockies into the western sections of the Southern Plains, and over the Eastern Seaboard and Southeast United States. This trough had focused numerous severe thunderstorms across the region on July 6th, with multiple outflow boundaries from these storms, coupled with ample moisture, large scale forcing along the upper trough itself, and renewed daytime heating which yielded strong instability, focusing shower and thunderstorm development during the morning and afternoon hours on the 7th across East Texas and North Louisiana. Some of these storms became severe, producing damaging winds that downed trees, an isolated instance of large hail, as well as heavy rainfall that led to localized flash flooding in Smith County throughout the cities of Tyler and Lindale, before diminishing late in the day.
